issues.issue: The collective definition of "Defendant" as both the holding company and the bank is plain and used consistently throughout paragraphs 1-18; nothing in it names an ambiguous term.

This recital says the parties resolved their claims "without the need for litigation", while the operative terms (paragraph 6 enforcement and paragraph 13 retained jurisdiction) contemplate contested enforcement proceedings in this Court. A party could invoke the recital to argue a narrower enforcement bargain than the operative text supplies.
The appeal waiver is conditioned on the judgment being "entered as submitted by the parties", a condition whose satisfaction (e.g. entry with any modification by the Court) is left undefined.

The appeal waiver interlocks with paragraph 14, which makes the Effective Date turn on there being "no party with a right to appeal"; the two must be read together to know when the judgment becomes effective.

"Those facts deemed necessary to the jurisdiction of this Court" is not identified, and neither the actor doing the deeming nor the set of admitted facts can be fixed from the text. A dispute over what Defendant has conceded would turn on that phrase.

"Without this Consent Judgment constituting evidence against Defendant" states no limits on the proceedings or purposes for which the bar operates, so its reach (third-party suits? enforcement proceedings?) is open.

The no-evidence recital sits uneasily with paragraph 6, which incorporates the Servicing Standards and Consumer Relief Requirements "as the judgment of this Court" to be enforced against Defendant. Enforcement necessarily uses the judgment against Defendant.

"Shall comply with the Servicing Standards ... in accordance with their terms and Section A of Exhibit E" leaves open whether compliance is an absolute per-loan duty or is measured only by the aggregate metrics and error-rate thresholds of Exhibit E. That is the classic fight between a servicer and an enforcing party over what counts as a violation.

Read against paragraph 6, which makes the Servicing Standards enforceable "in accordance with the authorities provided in the Enforcement Terms", and paragraph 18, which gives the Exhibits priority, it is unclear whether Exhibit E's metrics and cure machinery displace the flat compliance duty stated here.

The antecedent of "which sum shall be known as the 'Direct Payment Settlement Amount'" is uncertain: it may denote Defendant's own $1,005,233,716 payment or the pooled fund after other institutions' money is added. The figure itself is also written with a decimal point rather than a comma.

Paragraphs 9 and 10 make both releases effective "upon payment of the Direct Payment Settlement Amount by Defendant", which Defendant cannot do if that term means the pooled sum contributed by all institutions as paragraph 3 appears to define it.

The Borrower Payment Amount is written "$1,489,813.925.00", a figure with two decimal points that cannot be read as written. Eligibility also turns on unstated criteria "set forth by the State members of the Monitoring Committee".

The relief figure is punctuated "$3.434.000.000" and the credit entitlement is left entirely to Exhibit D ("credit towards such obligation as described in Exhibit D"), so the amount and the measure of satisfaction are both uncertain on the face of the paragraph.

Paragraph 12 lets a party withdraw for failure to make "Consumer Relief Payments" as defined in Exhibit F, a term that does not match the consumer relief obligation as described here, leaving the trigger for withdrawal unclear.
"Shall be enforced in accordance with the authorities provided in the Enforcement Terms" does not say whether Exhibit E supplies the exclusive route to enforcement or merely one available route.

Read with paragraph 13, under which the Court "retains jurisdiction ... to enforce its terms", it is unclear whether a party may seek judicial enforcement directly or must first exhaust the Exhibit E process and the Monitor's role under paragraph 7.

The Monitoring Committee is given authority over "all aspects of this and all similar Consent Judgments", but "similar" and "all aspects" set no boundary on the delegated power. A dispute over the Committee's authority would turn on those words.

The release is triggered by "payment of the Direct Payment Settlement Amount by Defendant", but paragraph 3 defines that amount as Defendant's payment aggregated with funds from other institutions, so the condition may be one Defendant alone cannot satisfy.

As with paragraph 9, the state releases become effective on "payment of the Direct Payment Settlement Amount by Defendant", a term paragraph 3 appears to define as the pooled multi-institution fund rather than Defendant's own contribution.

The paragraph says Exhibit H obligations "are in addition to" all other obligations and then immediately carves out an offset for wrongful-foreclosure payments; the general additive rule and the specific offset pull against each other, and the scope of "a payment ... for a wrongful foreclosure" is undefined.

The offset operates against "any payment from the Borrower Payment Amount" under paragraph 4, whose distribution is governed by Exhibit C and the State members of the Monitoring Committee, leaving unclear how a federal SCRA payment is to be reduced by a state-administered payment.

The withdrawal right turns on failure to make "Consumer Relief Payments (as that term is defined in Exhibit F)", a defined term that does not appear in paragraph 5's description of the consumer relief obligation, so the triggering default is uncertain.

A party's unilateral power to "declare it null and void with respect to that party" cannot easily be squared with paragraph 13, under which this Consent Judgment "may be modified only by order of this Court".

Retention of jurisdiction "for the duration of this Consent Judgment" sits against paragraph 15, which extends the Court's jurisdiction six months past the Term for violations identified in the final Monitor Report, and against paragraph 12's unilateral withdrawal right.

The Effective Date depends on the judgment being "final and non-appealable", deemed satisfied "if there is no party with a right to appeal the order on the day it is entered" — a self-referential test that does not address intervenors or non-parties.

The paragraph says Defendant "shall have no further obligations" six months after the Term while simultaneously preserving the Court's power to enforce or remedy outstanding violations, and it does not say how a violation must be "identified in the final Monitor Report" to survive. Both the sunset and its exception are open to competing readings.

The extended post-Term jurisdiction here is broader than paragraph 13's retention of jurisdiction "for the duration of this Consent Judgment", and the reference to violations not "cured during the Term" imports Exhibit E's cure machinery referenced in paragraph 2.

A savings clause preserving Defendant's duty to "comply with applicable state and federal law" can be read to cut against the breadth of the releases in paragraphs 9 and 10 (Exhibits F and G), which release specified statutory claims.

The clause calls the operative judgment a "summary document" whose "sum and substance" is reflected herein and in the Exhibits, without saying whether extrinsic material is excluded; "conflict" between Exhibits and paragraphs 1-18 is likewise undefined.

Because the Exhibits are made to govern over paragraphs 1-18, this clause determines whether paragraph 2's flat compliance duty or Exhibit E's enforcement and metrics regime controls, and so is the hinge of any conflict argument in the instrument.
